testedPalettes.concept: Material culture, past societies and excavation

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.content: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology

MCCHEAM213.name: Greek Archaeology
MCCHEAM213.content: The invention of democracy in classical Greece changed the nature of community decision-making, perhaps forever. This process is reflected in the material culture of the period. By examining the archaeology of community & democracy in early-democratic Greece, this course goes in search of ancient lessons for the modern world.

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.content: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.content: Late-medieval and Renaissance art; Mannerism; Baroque and Rococo; Enlightenment and Romanticism; Realism and Impressionism; Post-Impressionism, Symbolism and Art Nouveau; Modernism and Cubism; Interwar art; Postwar and postmodern art; Contemporary art; Artistic form and historical context

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.content: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.content: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.content: Creation and divine succession myths; Myth and cultural power; Gender and exchange; Epic and tragedy; Women, war and narrative agency; Focalization; Hero structures and motifemes; Cross-cultural storytelling; Myth in text, image and performance; Reception and adaptation; Ovid's Metamorphoses

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.content: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.content: Concepts and theories of empire; Imperial rise, expansion and decline; Administration and succession; Military and economic structures; Imperial ideologies and legitimacy; Culture and empire; Ancient and medieval empires; European overseas empires; Modern Asian and Eurasian empires; American power; Contemporary and future empires; Imperial legacies

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.content: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.content: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination

testedPalettes.assessment: Introduction to World Archaeology develops artefact description and technical drawing, Greek Archaeology studies material evidence for early democracy, and Heritage & Ancient Democracy uses objects, literature and history to interpret Athenian political life. These courses form a substantial starting cluster. The remaining history and arts courses broaden context but cannot develop excavation, finds processing, or specialist artefact analysis in sequence.

testedPalettes.assessment: African Art & Heritage and Modern Art & Modern Museums supply substantial material on collecting, interpretation and exhibition. Other arts, media and historical courses develop public communication and source analysis. A heritage curriculum could be coherent, but it would centre on art, institutions and cultural interpretation, with too little of the archaeological evidence and methods that define this degree.

testedPalettes.assessment: Earth Observation and Spatial Planning teach GIS and spatial methods. Dynamic Earth teaches geological stratigraphy and field observation, and Soils & Aquifers adds sampling and laboratory techniques. These are useful transferable methods. They lack a progression that applies those techniques to archaeological deposits, sites, artefacts and finds documentation.

combinedCandidate: The strongest integrated response combines three substantive archaeology/material-culture courses with heritage, spatial analysis and Earth-science practicals. World Archaeology provides object description and technical drawing, Greek Archaeology uses material evidence to understand ancient political life, and Heritage and Ancient Democracy combines primary texts and archaeological material with civic interpretation. African Art and Heritage and Modern Art and Modern Museums add research on collections, interpretation and public exhibition. Description-only Greek Archaeology, Renaissance Italy and Global Mediterranean, and Writing Art’s Histories have real contributions in material evidence, art exchange and interpretive method. Earth Observation and description-only Spatial Planning teach GIS and remote sensing. Dynamic Earth provides geological stratigraphy and field measurement. Soils and Aquifers adds field sampling and environmental laboratories. Digital imaging and data science also contribute transferable methods. The combined palette lacks repeated excavation and recording of human deposits, finds processing, disciplinary materials analysis and the research-to-publication progression. Filling out 24 courses would materially shift the centre to heritage, general humanities or environmental science. None of the three candidates sustains sufficient archaeology as a whole programme. This judgment follows course content independently of terms and availability.
